vignette:
Kwame is a twenty-year-old doctor who grew up in a small village in West Africa before emigrating to the United States for medical training. He is the youngest physician in his hospital’s emergency department, a fact that once filled him with pride but now feels like a cruel joke. The trauma that reshaped his life occurred eighteen months ago, during a humanitarian mission in a conflict zone near his home region. His convoy was ambushed. He remembers the sudden silence after the first explosion—the way the world went still, the air thick with dust and the sharp smell of cordite. He remembers the chaos that followed: the wounded, the shouting, the desperate pressure of his hands on a soldier’s chest as the man’s breathing slowed, then stopped. What he cannot remember, no matter how hard he tries, is the moment between the blast and the silence. There are gaps—minutes, maybe hours—that feel like a black hole in his mind. The memory comes only in fragments: a hand reaching for him, a scream that might have been his own, the weight of a body he could not save. He pushes the memory away before it can fully form, as though his brain has learned to slam a door before the nightmare can walk through.

In the months since, Kwame has become a stranger to himself. He used to be calm, decisive, the colleague others relied on in a crisis. Now he is jumpy, irritable, and haunted by the belief that the world is fundamentally unsafe. His shattered beliefs are not abstract—they are lived, daily. He no longer trusts that a quiet emergency room will stay quiet, that a patient’s stable vitals will remain stable. He is certain that violence can erupt at any moment, and that he will fail to stop it. This hypervigilance has become his default state; he scans every room for exits, every face for threat, every silence for the sound of an explosion. The triggers are everywhere, but the most devastating is breathlessness. When he runs up the stairs to the trauma bay, when a mask is placed over a patient’s face, when he himself feels short of breath after a long shift, the sensation slams him back into that moment of suffocating helplessness. Each time, his appraisals harden further: he is not the person he thought he was. He is weak, broken, no longer fit to be a doctor.

The cycle is relentless. The triggers—especially breathlessness and sudden silence—reinforce his belief that he is permanently changed and that the world is dangerous. And those beliefs, in turn, make him more sensitive to triggers: he now dreads the quiet of the on-call room, the hush that falls before a code blue, the still air of a patient’s room late at night. The memory itself feeds this loop. When a fragment surfaces—the soldier’s pale face, the wet sound of a breath that would not come—he is flooded with shame and fear, which only deepens his conviction that he has lost himself. He has come to believe that remembering fully would destroy him, so he blocks it, but the blocking leaves him with only disjointed pieces that feel more like accusations than memories. Each piece reinforces his negative appraisals, and each appraisal makes the next trigger more potent.

His work has become a minefield. He avoids the trauma bay when he can, trading shifts with colleagues, claiming fatigue. He has stopped responding to codes unless absolutely necessary. The silence of the recovery room, where patients lie still and breathing, has become unbearable. He now takes the stairs instead of the elevator, not for exercise but because the enclosed space and the quiet remind him too much of the aftermath of the ambush. One consequence is that his relationships with colleagues have frayed. He was once the youngest doctor everyone admired; now he is the one who makes excuses, who disappears during handoffs, who seems distant and cold. He knows they talk. He knows they wonder. What frightens him most is that they might be right.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment in the resuscitation bay three weeks ago. A teenager was brought in after a car accident, unconscious, breathing shallowly. Kwame placed the oxygen mask over the boy’s face and watched his chest rise and fall. The room went quiet. For a second—just a second—Kwame could not move. He felt his own throat close, his own breath stop. He froze, and a senior nurse had to push him aside. No one said anything, but Kwame saw the look on her face. That night, he could not sleep. He sat in his apartment, listening to the hum of the refrigerator, and realized he was afraid of everything: afraid of the silence, afraid of the next shift, afraid of the person he had become. He is hoping—though he is not sure he believes it—that there is a way back to who he was.
